title: Cap. X Arg. X cont.: if 1 Cor. iv. 7 holds of gratia gratis data, much more of justifying grace and of the first grace of election to life
latin: Si hoc in gratia gratis data (ut Schola loquitur) verum sit, tum multo magis in gratia gratum faciente, et maxime omnium in prima illa gratia electionis ad vitam, quae fons est et quasi scaturigo beneficiorum omnium ad salutem conferentium.
pass_a: If this be true in grace freely given (as the School speaks), then much more in grace that makes acceptable, and most of all in that first grace of election unto life, which is the fountain and as it were the spring of all benefits conferring unto salvation.
pass_b: If that holds of gratia gratis data, as the School calls it, it holds much more of the grace that makes acceptable—and most of all of that first grace of election to life, the fountain and spring of every benefit that serves salvation.

lemmas.gloss: from gratis data up to justifying grace
election-to-life as fountain of saving gifts

title: Cap. X Arg. X: Augustine De praedest. sanct. 5 — common gifts do not discern; the grace that discerns good from evil is not common; God discerns you from another
latin: Sed audiamus Augustinum Pauli vestigiis et doctrinae inhaerentem: De praedest. sanct. cap. 5. Numquid, inquit, per haec dona, quae omnibus communia sunt hominibus, discernuntur homines ab hominibus? Paulo post, Gratia quae bonos discernit a malis, non communis est et bonis et malis. Adhuc planius; Deus te discernit ab alio, cui non donavit, quod donavit tibi.
pass_a: But let us hear Augustine cleaving to Paul’s footsteps and doctrine: De praedest. sanct. cap. 5. Are men, he says, discerned from men by these gifts which are common unto all men? A little after, The grace which discerns the good from the evil is not common both unto the good and unto the evil. Yet more plainly; God discerns thee from another, unto whom he has not given what he has given unto thee.
pass_b: Hear Augustine keeping Paul’s steps and teaching (De praedestinatione sanctorum 5): Are men set apart from men by gifts common to all? A little later: The grace that sets the good apart from the evil is not common to both. Still plainer: God sets you apart from another, to whom he has not given what he gave you.

lemmas.gloss: common gifts do not discern persons

title: Cap. X Arg. X: elect/non-elect divide arises from God’s diverse decrees of preparing and giving—not from human operations about commonly offered grace; Arminius intolerable
latin: Ex quibus omnibus manifestum est, Discrimen electorum et non-electorum, credentium et non-credentium, perseverantium et non-perseverantium oriri non ex antecedaneis et discretis humanarum voluntatum circa gratiam communiter oblatam operationibus, sed ex antecedaneis et diversis Dei decretis et operationibus, in decernendo, praeparando et donando uni quod non decrevit, neque praeparavit neque donavit alteri. Intoleranda est igitur Arminii sententia, quae ad Deum refert communem quandam gratiae praeparationem et oblationem, ad singulorum autem hominum liberum arbitrium hac communi gratia excitatum refert ipsam discriminationem credentium et non-credentium, electorum et non-electorum.
pass_a: From all which it is manifest that The discrimination of elect and non-elect, of believing and not-believing, of persevering and not-persevering arises not from antecedent and discrete operations of human wills about grace commonly offered, but from antecedent and diverse decrees and operations of God, in decreeing, preparing, and giving unto one what he has not decreed, nor prepared, nor given unto the other. Intolerable therefore is Arminius’s sentence, which refers unto God a certain common preparation and offer of grace, but refers unto the free will of singular men, stirred by this common grace, the very discrimination of believers and non-believers, elect and non-elect.
pass_b: From all this it is plain: the divide of elect and non-elect, believers and unbelievers, those who persevere and those who do not, does not arise from prior, distinct human-will operations about commonly offered grace, but from God’s prior, diverse decrees and workings—decreeing, preparing, and giving to one what he neither decreed nor prepared nor gave to the other. So Arminius’s view is intolerable: it credits God with a common preparation and offer of grace, but credits each person’s free will, stirred by that common grace, with the very discrimination of believers and unbelievers, elect and non-elect.

title: Cap. X Arg. X Major/Minor: non-elect = those to whom God never destined efficacious means; many such exist; therefore many are passed by before foresight of final unbelief
latin: Quod attinet ad vitam aeternam, ille antecedenter ad praevisam suam infidelitatem praeteritus, non-electus, sive reprobatus consideratur, cui Deus ab aeterno non destinavit, praeparavit, ac cui in tempore non donavit efficacia media ad fidem et perseverantiam ingenerandam, vitamque aeternam infallibiliter obtinendam: At multis (sicut eventus ipse declarat) Deus nec destinavit, nec praeparavit, nec donavit hanc gratiam efficacem. Ergo, multi sunt praeteriti sive non-electi antecedenter ad praevisam suam infidelitatem et contumaciam finalem in eadem. De Minore nulla potest esse quaestio: Majorem igitur explicemus et confirmemus.
pass_a: As concerns everlasting life, he is considered passed by, non-elect, or reprobate antecedently unto his foreseen unbelief, unto whom God from eternity has not destined, prepared, and unto whom in time he has not given efficacious means unto begetting faith and perseverance, and infallibly obtaining everlasting life: But unto many (as the event itself declares) God has neither destined, nor prepared, nor given this efficacious grace. Therefore many are passed by or non-elect antecedently unto their foreseen unbelief and final contumacy in the same. Concerning the Minor there can be no question: let us therefore unfold and confirm the Major.
pass_b: As for everlasting life: the one passed by, non-elect, or reprobate before foresight of his unbelief is the one to whom God from eternity neither destined nor prepared, and in time did not give, efficacious means to beget faith and perseverance and obtain everlasting life infallibly. But to many—as the event itself shows—God neither destined nor prepared nor gave that efficacious grace. Therefore many are passed by or non-elect before foresight of their unbelief and final stubbornness in it. The Minor is beyond dispute; so let us open and confirm the Major.

title: Cap. X Arg. X Major: God knows infinite modes to turn any heart; to deny this denies omnipotence — Prov. xxi. 1; Augustine De corr. et grat. 14
latin: Illud imprimis sumo; Deum nosse infinitos modos quibus cor cujuscunque hominis flectere possit ad libere poenitendum, credendum, et perseverandum. Qui hoc negat, negat Dei omnipotentiam, negat Dei supra voluntates humanas absolutum dominium, contra illud Solomonis, Cor regis in manu Domini; quocunque voluerit inclinavit illud, Prov. xxi. 1. Cui subscribit Augustinus, De corrept. et gratia, cap. 14. De ipsis hominum voluntatibus facit quod vult, et quando vult, habens humanorum cordium quo vult inclinandorum omnipotentissimam potestatem.
pass_a: That first I take; that God knows infinite modes by which he can bend the heart of any man unto freely repenting, believing, and persevering. Who denies this denies God’s omnipotence, denies God’s absolute dominion over human wills, against that of Solomon, The king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord; whithersoever he will he has inclined it, Prov. xxi. 1. Unto which Augustine subscribes, De corrept. et gratia, cap. 14. Of the very wills of men he does what he wills, and when he wills, having the most omnipotent power of inclining human hearts whithersoever he wills.
pass_b: First I take this: God knows infinite ways to bend any man’s heart to repent, believe, and persevere freely. Who denies it denies God’s omnipotence and his absolute lordship over human wills—against Solomon (Prov. xxi. 1): The king’s heart is in the Lord’s hand; he turns it wherever he wills. Augustine subscribes (De correptione et gratia 14): Of men’s very wills he does what he wills, when he wills, holding most omnipotent power to incline human hearts wherever he wills.

lemmas.gloss: infinite modes to turn any heart
Prov. xxi.1 heart in Lord’s hand

title: Cap. X Arg. X: he who could bend Judas as Peter, yet destined the means to Peter not Judas, elected one and reprobated the other — Ambrose: God calls whom he deigns
latin: Hisce addo, Illum qui novit et potuit adhibere tam Judae quam Petro ea media, quibus ad fidem et obedientiam flecteretur, et in fide et obedientia ad extremum usque conservaretur, atque haec media Petro ab aeterno destinavit et donavit, Judae nec destinavit nec donavit, unum eorum elegisse ad salutem, alterum praeteriisse, id est, reprobasse. Hoc illud est quod Ambrosius celebri illo dicto innuabat, Deus quos dignatur vocat, et quem vult religiosum facit. Quae verba accurate expenduntur ab Augustino, De grat. Christi contra Pelag. et Caelest. lib. 1. cap. 46.
pass_a: Unto these I add, That he who knew and could apply unto Judas as unto Peter those means by which he would be bent unto faith and obedience, and conserved in faith and obedience unto the very end, and from eternity destined and gave these means unto Peter, unto Judas neither destined nor gave them, elected one of them unto salvation, passed by the other, that is, reprobated him. This is that which Ambrose hinted by that celebrated saying, God calls whom he deigns, and makes religious whom he wills. Which words are accurately weighed by Augustine, De grat. Christi contra Pelag. et Caelest. lib. 1. cap. 46.
pass_b: Add this: he who knew and could apply to Judas as to Peter the means to bend him to faith and obedience and keep him in them to the end, yet from eternity destined and gave those means to Peter and neither destined nor gave them to Judas, elected one to salvation and passed the other by—that is, reprobated him. That is what Ambrose meant in the famous saying: God calls whom he deigns, and makes religious whom he wills—words Augustine weighs carefully (De gratia Christi contra Pelagium et Caelestium 1.46).

title: Cap. X Arg. X: Basil and Isa. xlvi. — when God wills he saves and none resists; those not effectually called lack that unfrustrable will to convert and save
latin: Hisce consonat illud Basilii, in oratione quadam quae refertur a Petro Diacono, lib. De incarn. et grat. cap. 8. Dona, Domine, virtutem ac tutamentum. Malos, quos sumis, bonos facito; bonos in bonitate conservato: omnia enim potes, et non est qui contradicat tibi. Cum enim volueris, salvas, et non est qui resistat tibi. Uterque a Propheta hoc didicit, qui de voluntate divina ita nos instituit, Isa. xlvi. 10 et 11. Juravit Dominus exercituum, Si non ut putavi ita erit, et quomodo mente tractavi ita eveniet. Dominus exercituum decrevit, et quis poterit infirmare? Ex hisce omnibus infero, quod eos qui non vocantur vocatione efficaci, et qui religiosi non efficiuntur, qui non in fide et sancta obedientia conservantur; uno verbo, qui reapse non salvantur, defuisse Deo illam voluntatem et infrustrabilem eos convertendi, religiosos et fideles efficiendi, in fide conservandi, atque tandem de facto salvandi.
pass_a: Unto these agrees that of Basil, in a certain oration which is reported by Peter the Deacon, lib. De incarn. et grat. cap. 8. Give, O Lord, virtue and safeguard. Make good the evil whom thou takest; conserve the good in goodness: for thou canst all things, and there is none who contradicts thee. For when thou hast willed, thou savest, and there is none who resists thee. Both learned this from the Prophet, who thus instructs us concerning the divine will, Isa. xlvi. 10 and 11. The Lord of hosts has sworn, If it shall not be as I have thought, and as I have handled it in mind, so shall it come to pass. The Lord of hosts has decreed, and who shall be able to weaken it? From all these I infer that unto those who are not called with an efficacious calling, and who are not made religious, who are not conserved in faith and holy obedience; in a word, who are not in very deed saved, there has been wanting unto God that will and unfrustrable will of converting them, of making them religious and faithful, of conserving them in faith, and at length of saving them in fact.
pass_b: Basil agrees, in an oration Peter the Deacon reports (De incarnatione et gratia 8): Give, Lord, strength and safeguard. Make good the evil you take; keep the good in goodness—for you can do all things, and none contradicts you. When you will, you save, and none resists you. Both learned it from the Prophet on the divine will (Isa. xlvi. 10–11): The Lord of hosts has sworn: It shall be as I thought; as I planned in mind, so it shall happen. The Lord of hosts has decreed—and who can weaken it? From all this I infer: for those not called with an efficacious call, not made religious, not kept in faith and holy obedience—in a word, not actually saved—God lacked that unfrustrable will to convert them, make them religious and faithful, keep them in faith, and at last save them in fact.

lemmas.gloss: Basil: when God wills he saves; none resists
non-saved lack God’s unfrustrable saving will

title: Cap. X Arg. X close toward Corvinus: opposite for the elect — eternal saving will proves election/preterition; foresight cannot ground either special will or its denial
latin: sicut e contra, quoad eos qui religiosi, fideles, perseverantes efficiuntur, et ad vitam aeternam perducuntur, colligere possumus ab aeterno adfuisse Deo illam voluntatem, quae haec omnia in illis efficaciter operaretur. Haec autem voluntas salvandi, et noluntas (si ita loqui liceat) electionem aliquorum et praeteritionem aliorum manifeste evincit. Denique, sicut ineptum esset obtendere hanc specialem voluntatem de fide, perseverantia et salute Petri operanda ex praevisa ejusdem Petri fide et perseverantia profluxisse, ita non minus falsum et ineptum est asserere, hanc negatam voluntatem efficiendi fidem, poenitentiam et perseverantiam in Juda, aut quolibet reprobato, ex praevisa ejusdem infidelitate, impoenitentia et finali gratiae Divinae contemptu originem habuisse.
pass_a: just as on the contrary, as concerns those who are made religious, faithful, persevering, and are led unto everlasting life, we can gather that from eternity that will was present unto God which would efficaciously work all these things in them. But this will of saving, and non-will (if one may so speak) manifestly proves the election of some and the preterition of others. Finally, just as it would be inept to pretend that this special will of working faith, perseverance, and salvation in Peter flowed from foresight of the same Peter’s faith and perseverance, so it is no less false and inept to assert that this denied will of effecting faith, repentance, and perseverance in Judas, or in any reprobate, had its origin from foresight of the same man’s unbelief, impenitence, and final contempt of Divine grace.
pass_b: Conversely, of those made religious, faithful, persevering, and led to everlasting life, we may gather that from eternity God had that will which would efficaciously work all this in them. That will to save—and non-will, if one may so speak—plainly proves election of some and preterition of others. Finally: as it would be inept to claim that the special will to work faith, perseverance, and salvation in Peter flowed from foresight of Peter’s faith and perseverance, so it is no less false and inept to assert that the denied will to effect faith, repentance, and perseverance in Judas or any reprobate arose from foresight of his unbelief, impenitence, and final contempt of divine grace.

lemmas.gloss: denied will not from foresight of unbelief
